evidence.text: A shoot 屮 growing in the soil 土
Pictograph of a sprout emerging from the ground.
進也。象艸木生出土上。凡生之屬皆从生。

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 屮 (“bud”) + 一 (“ground”) – sprouting from the ground. A conservative version is 𤯓, which is unrelated to 㞷 (匩 > 匡) and 𡴀 > 丰.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sreŋ (“to live; to be alive; to give birth; raw; green”). Cognate with Burmese ရှင် (hrang, “to live; alive”), Mizo hring (“to bear; to bring forth; to give birth to; green”).
Schuessler (2007) proposes that Proto-Sino-Tibetan *sriŋ is derived from the root *sri (“to exist”) (whence possibly Chinese 體 (OC *r̥ʰiːʔ, “body; shape; form”)) + *-ŋ (terminative suffix).
Both level tone and falling tone readings are found in Middle Chinese, but the latter has since been lost and is merged into the level-tone reading in modern dialects.
Related to 青 (OC *sʰleːŋ, “blue-green”), 蒼 (OC *sʰaːŋ, *sʰaːŋʔ, “dark blue; deep green”).
Derivatives: 性 (OC *sleŋs, “nature; character; personality; quality”), 姓 (OC *sleŋs, “family name”).
Pronunciation in Early Middle Chinese is *sraeng, but it comes from an earlier *srjaeng, as seen in Wang Renxu's edition of the Qieyun.
From Mandarin 上.
Phono-semantic matching of Japanese さん (-san).
進也。象艸木生出土上。凡生之屬皆从生。

evidence.field: 形義通解: graphic formation and evolution
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 生 as 屮 (a sprout) above 一 representing ground, expressing a plant growing out of earth. It says early bronze forms continue the oracle-bone structure; a dot was later added beneath 屮 as a decorative stroke and then became a horizontal stroke, making it resemble 土. Seal script retains the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. The entry treats Shuowen’s gloss 進也 as an extended sense, rather than the graphic core.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone examples: 合集34078 uses 生 in a prayer for childbirth; 合集8648正 生月 is interpreted as the following month; 合集116正 uses 生 adjectivally of fresh/live birds; 合集10270 refers to a live deer. These show early uses, but the entry’s proposed semantic connection between the following-month sense and life/growth is an interpretation, not a demonstrated chronological derivation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.field: 形義通解: bronze and Warring States uses
evidence.text: For bronze inscriptions, the entry cites 生 meaning give birth in 叔尸鐘, occur/produce in 中山王方壺, living in 中方鼎, lifespan in 蔡姞簋, and as a phonetic loan for 姓 on 兮甲盤. It cites Warring States manuscripts for childbirth in 清華簡二《繫年》 and living opposed to dying in 上博竹書一《緇衣》 slip 19. The cited examples establish attested uses; they do not by themselves order all senses into a chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.text: The related 姓 entry says 生 supplies sound in 姓, alongside 女 in oracle-bone forms and 人 in bronze forms; it also reports that oracle-bone 生 can be read as 姓 in 多生, while giving 多甥 as an alternative proposal. This is a whole-graph phonetic borrowing/use and is distinct from 生’s role as a complete graph. No component-level phonetic analysis applies to 生 itself here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：oracle-piece entry for 生 and 姓

evidence.source: 許慎《說文解字》, as transcribed in 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The entry transcribes 說文:「進也。象艸木生出土上。凡生之屬皆从生。」The historical lexicographic account describes plants emerging above soil; the modern paleographic entry interprets 進 as an extended sense. Shuowen is a historical source and does not independently prove every detail of the earlier oracle-bone structure.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：生

evidence.source: Che-mao Tsai, Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica
evidence.field: article metadata and abstracted discussion of 生月
evidence.text: Tsai’s 1993 article record identifies the study as 卜辭生字再探, published in Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology 64.8, pp. 1047–1076. The accessible page discusses disagreement over 生月: it presents the established ‘following month’ analysis and argues from lunar waxing/waning, while other readings have taken 生月 as ‘this month’ or questioned the reading. This is a disputed lexical interpretation; it does not establish the character’s graphic origin.
evidence.title: 卜辭生字再探 A New Look at the Character ‘sheng’ in Oracle Bone Inscriptions

evidence.source: Che-mao Tsai, Fudan University Center for Unearthed Documents and Paleography
evidence.text: Tsai argues that oracle-bone 生月 means the next month, relating it to the moon beginning to grow again, and rejects an alternative reading of the month graph as 夕 in the cited context. The argument concerns interpretation of an oracle-bone phrase; it is not proof that ‘next month’ was the earliest meaning of 生.
evidence.title: 蔡哲茂：卜辭生字再探

evidence.text: The supplied local rows give 生 modern pinyin shēng; Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese sraeng (also srjaeng in one row); Old Chinese *sreŋ, with row-specific glosses ‘bear, be born; live’ and ‘fresh, raw’ and explicit uncertainty in one row (*sreŋ (MC srj- > sr-; or *s.reŋ ?)). evidence.field: 生 detailed senses and historical citation examples
evidence.text: The entry separates growth, giving birth/raising, living opposite death, and producing/occurring into separate senses, illustrating them with citations to classical works including 詩, 左傳, 論語, 孫子, and 孟子. This lexicographic list documents later lexical range but is not used to infer chronological order among senses.
evidence.title: 生 shēng - 漢典

evidence.field: oracle-bone graph formation and graphic development
evidence.text: The entry analyzes oracle-bone 生 as 屮 over 一, with 一 representing ground: a plant growing from the soil. It says early bronze forms retain this structure; a dot was later added below 屮 as a decorative stroke and became a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土. Small seal retains the sprout-emerging-from-ground idea. This is a modern paleographic analysis, not a claim that every early variant is visually identical.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—生

evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—生

evidence.text: The entry cites oracle-bone 生 in a prayer for childbirth (合集34078), 生月 in 合集8648正, and adjectivally for live/fresh birds (合集116正) and a live deer (合集10270). It reports 生月 as ‘following month’ and 生 in 多生 as 姓, while noting an alternative analysis 多甥. These cited examples establish reported usages, not a chronology among them; the 生月 interpretation remains disputed.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—生

evidence.text: The entry cites bronze 生 for childbirth in 叔尸鐘, occur/produce in 中山王方壺, a living creature in 中方鼎, lifespan in 蔡姞簋, and as a phonetic loan for 姓 on 兮甲盤. It also cites Warring States manuscripts for childbirth in 清華簡二《繫年》 and living opposed to dying in 上博竹書一《緇衣》 slip 19. The entry supplies no artifact date for each cited token, so none is assigned here; the examples do not order senses chronologically.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—生

evidence.text: The related 姓 entry says 生 supplies sound in 姓; oracle-bone 姓 has 女 plus 生, while bronze 姓 has 人 plus 生. It separately reports oracle-bone 生 used for 姓 in 多生, with 多甥 offered as an alternative. This concerns 生 as a whole graph borrowed/used for another word, distinct from 屮’s semantic role within 生. The pronunciation and reconstruction rows supplied locally show 生 and 姓 modern Mandarin shēng and xìng, and Baxter–Sagart MC sraeng/sjengH and OC *sreŋ (variant row-specific notation)/*seŋ-s; these comparisons alone do not establish the historical borrowing.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

items.caption: This oracle-script form shows a central stalk with two shoots above a horizontal ground line, illustrating the analysis of 生 as a sprout emerging from soil.
items.alt: Black glyph with an upright central stalk and two curved shoots rising above a horizontal base.
items.selection_reason: The visible sprout and ground line make the proposed graphic interpretation clear.
items.rights: Commons description labels the representation public domain and identifies the Sinica source image as CC0 1.0.

items.period: Western Zhou bronze style; description links 七年趞曹鼎 and calls it mid Western Zhou
items.caption: This bronze-script form is analyzed as retaining the sprout-over-ground structure. The account describes a lower mark beneath the sprout becoming a horizontal stroke in later forms.
items.alt: Black glyph with an upright, branching upper shape, a narrow middle stem, and a broad, irregular lower stroke.
items.selection_reason: It adds a bronze-script example that supports the sprout-over-ground analysis and helps explain the account of change in the lower part of the graph.
items.rights: Commons description states that the Sinica source picture is CC0 1.0; Commons labels the vector representation public domain.

limitations.text: These modern vector renderings illustrate the proposed graphic analysis, but do not establish a dated sequence of individual artifacts or show that every recorded meaning of 生 developed from the sprout image.
